items.title: NostradamusGPT: The Psychology of Prophecy and How to Break Free from the Prison of Predictive Technologies
items.description: This is our paradox: We know that uncertainty is the substrate of the universe, is the crucible of creativity, is the path to truth, and yet we spend our lives searching for certainty. The word auspicious derives from the Latin auspex — one who examines the flight of birds for omens and divinations of the future. items.title: James Baldwin on How Love (Finally) Finds You
items.description: Our language betrays our self-betrayals: We speak of finding love, as if it were an undiscovered eighth continent or a habitable world in another solar system, as if it got lost like the Little Red Riding Hood or the names of the women who painted the caves. items.title: Hermann Hesse on How to Read a Book and How to Read Yourself
items.description: Books show us what it is like to be another and at the same time return us to ourselves. We read to learn how to live — how to love and how to suffer, how to grieve and how to be glad. We read to clarify ourselves and to anneal our values. We read for the assurance that others have lived through what we are living through. “You think your pain and your heartbreak are unprecedented in the history of the world, but then you read,” James Baldwin reflected in his most personal interview. items.title: Sleeping Beauties: David Byrne on Why Transformative Ideas Fall Dormant and How They Awaken to Change the World
items.description: Each time you look up at the night sky, you see only ancient signals — by the time a photon has reached your pupil, the star that emitted it may be long dead. The great wonder is that its light can traverse immense expanses of space and time to gladden the darkness of today, to cast wonder upon this lonely planet. An idea is a signal that may travel across immense expanses of space and time before it touches the world. Transformative ideas can and often do fall on the closed eyes of their epoch.

items.title: How to Hold Your Helplessness: Nobel Laureate Bertrand Russell’s Salve for the Anxiety of Overwhelm
items.description: "A way of life cannot be successful so long as it is a mere intellectual conviction. It must be deeply felt, deeply believed, dominant even in dreams."

items.title: Elizabeth Gilbert on Love, Loss, and How to Move Through Grief as Grief Moves Through You
items.description: "Grief is a force of energy that cannot be controlled or predicted. It comes and goes on its own schedule. Grief does not obey your plans, or your wishes. Grief will do whatever it wants to you, whenever it wants to. In that regard, Grief has a lot in common with Love."

items.title: How to Remake Yourself When You Are Undone: Lincoln and the Gift of His Suicidal Depression
items.description: Life-affirming inspiration from a man who knew intimately “that intensity of thought, which will some times wear the sweetest idea thread-bare and turn it to the bitterness of death.”

items.title: How to Doubt Your Way into a Truer Life
items.description: The most maddening thing about life is also the most beautiful: its indeterminacy. The course of our lives, the fate of our species, the future of the universe: all undecided. items.title: How Memory Makes Us and Breaks Truth: The Rashomon Effect and the Science of How Memories Form and Falter in the Brain
items.description: "We are our memory… that chimerical museum of shifting shapes, that pile of broken mirrors.”

items.title: Nobel Laureate Doris Lessing on Breaking Free from the Prisons We Choose to Live Inside
items.description: This is the history of the world: revolutionaries turning into tyrants, leaders who claim to stand with the masses turning the individuals within them on each other, stirring certainties and self-righteousness to distract from the uncomfortable unknowns, from the great open question of what makes us and keeps us human, and human together. items.title: An Introvert’s Field Guide to Friendship: Thoreau on the Challenges and Rewards of Candid Connection
items.description: "We only need to be as true to others as we are to ourselves that there may be ground enough for friendship."

items.title: Probability Theory Pioneer Mark Kac on the Unpredictability of Creativity and the Two Types of Geniuses
items.description: "Creative people live in two worlds. One is the ordinary world which they share with others and in which they are not in any special way set apart from their fellow men. The other is private and it is in this world that the creative acts take place."
